messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Final Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a moderate traumatic brain injury, stigmas of trauma in the anterior chest wall, and signs of respiratory distress after falling off a cliff while riding his bicycle. Upon admission, a thoracoabdominal computed tomography angiography reported pneumomediastinum, a small right pneumothorax, and an image of loss of continuity in the anterior superior wall of the right main bronchus highly suggestive of bronchial rupture. The bronchial lesion was confirmed by fiberoptic bronchoscopy, showing a linear 1-cm rupture at the level of the root of the right main bronchus, in its lateral aspect, with fracture of the entire bronchial wall. Conservative management was chosen, and the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) with protective tracheal intubation. The patient’s ICU stay included a respiratory rate of 12 breaths per minute, tidal volume of 6–8 ml/kg, I/E 1:3, PEEP 5 cm H2O, and plateau pressure of < 30 mmHg. After 48 hours, the pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum resolved spontaneously, with limited subcutaneous emphysema, and the patient was successfully extubated on day 4. Strict follow-up was performed without evidence of swallowing or respiratory disorders, which allowed for the patient’s discharge 1 week later.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient is considered stable with no evidence of respiratory or swallowing disorders.

Follow-Up Plans:
Patient will follow-up in 4-6 weeks for scheduled evaluation.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for the admission is a traumatic rupture of the right main bronchus from the bicycle fall. It was confirmed on bronchoscopy, needed ICU care with protective intubation, and also explains the pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum. This is an injury of an intrathoracic organ (bronchus), which is chapter S, category S27.

CODE: S27
